title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

reading.body:
An attorney used an AI tool to generate case citations in a legal brief without checking them against actual court records. Two of the citations were entirely fabricated, and a quotation from a real case was falsified. The opposing attorney caught the errors before the judge, who ruled against the attorney's client and imposed sanctions.

This is a failure of verification at the point of deployment. The attorney presented AI-generated content as factual law in a court filing without the human review that legal practice requires. A basic check against a legal database would have caught both the invented cases and the misquoted precedent before the brief was filed.

It is not established whether this was the first time the attorney had used an AI tool for legal work, or what training or warnings about AI limitations he had received.

reports.title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

summary:
Minnesota attorney Faisal S. Ahmed was suspended for 30 days after citing fake court cases in legal documents filed in Hennepin County Court. Ahmed used an AI tool to draft a brief for a client involved in a civil dispute over unpaid rent and included two entirely fabricated case citations, Anderson v. City of Biwabik and Doherty v. Alma E. Clark Memorial Home, along with a false quotation from an actual case. The opposing attorney discovered the errors and alerted Judge Lois Conroy, who ruled against Ahmed's client and ordered the defendants to pay $233,563 in back rent. Ahmed also faced a $5,000 fine from the court.

The Minnesota Lawyer's Professional Responsibility Board filed disciplinary action against Ahmed on Friday, and he agreed to the 30-day license suspension plus an additional $900 in costs. Judge Conroy noted that over 800 documented instances of AI-generated fake legal citations have been catalogued on a dedicated website. This incident follows similar cases in Minnesota courts where attorneys used ChatGPT that produced false citations, prompting state officials to remind lawyers that their ethical obligations apply to all use of artificial intelligence tools.
